content: Asthma exacerbations can occur frequently and vary in severity, ranging from mild to life-threatening. Magnesium sulfate (MgSO₄) is one of several treatment options available for managing acute asthma exacerbations. While the efficacy of intravenous MgSO₄ has been well-established, the role of inhaled MgSO₄ remains less clear. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of inhaled MgSO₄ in the treatment of acute asthma. Specifically, the review aimed to assess the effects of inhaled MgSO₄ when used in addition to a combination of inhaled β₂-agonists and ipratropium bromide, when used alongside inhaled β₂-agonists alone, and when compared directly to inhaled β₂-agonists. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were identified through a systematic search of the Cochrane Airways Group register of trials and online trial registries as of September 2017. Additional studies were identified by reviewing reference lists of published articles and contacting trial authors. Eligible studies included adults or children with acute asthma who were treated with nebulized MgSO₄ either alone or in combination with β₂-agonists and/or ipratropium bromide. Comparisons were made against the same co-interventions without MgSO₄ or against an inactive control. Two independent reviewers assessed the trials for inclusion, extracted data, and evaluated the risk of bias. Missing data were sought from study authors. Results were presented as mean differences (MDs) or standardized mean differences (SMDs) for pulmonary function, clinical severity scores, and vital signs, and as risk ratios (RRs) for hospital admissions. Risk differences (RDs) were used to analyze adverse events due to their rarity. A total of 25 trials, encompassing 43 references and involving 2907 randomized patients (2777 completed), were included. The studies varied in methodological quality, design, definitions, interventions, and outcomes, making direct comparisons challenging. The quality of evidence ranged from high to very low, with most outcomes graded as low or very low due to methodological concerns and imprecision in pooled estimates. Inhaled MgSO₄ in addition to inhaled β₂-agonists and ipratropium bromide: Seven studies were included in this comparison. While some individual studies reported improvements in lung function favoring the intervention group, the overall results were inconsistent. The largest study found no significant difference in predicted peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) at 60 minutes (MD −0.3%, 95% CI −2.71% to 2.11%). Hospital admissions at initial presentation may be slightly reduced with the addition of inhaled MgSO₄ (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.00; participants = 1308; studies = 4; I² = 52%), but no differences were observed for re-admissions or escalation of care to intensive or high-dependency units. Serious adverse events during admission were rare, and there was no significant difference in overall adverse events between groups (RD 0.01, 95% CI −0.03 to 0.05; participants = 1197; studies = 2). Inhaled MgSO₄ in addition to inhaled β₂-agonists: Thirteen studies were included in this comparison. Although some individual studies reported improvements in lung function favoring the intervention group, pooled results did not demonstrate a conclusive benefit as measured by forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV₁) or PEFR. Pooled results for hospital admissions showed a point estimate favoring the combination of MgSO₄ and β₂-agonists, but the confidence interval included the possibility of increased admissions in the intervention group (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.52 to 1.15; participants = 375; studies = 6; I² = 0%). No serious adverse events were reported, and there was no significant difference in overall adverse events between groups (RD −0.01, 95% CI −0.05 to 0.03; participants = 694; studies = 5). Inhaled MgSO₄ versus inhaled β₂-agonists: Four studies were included in this comparison. The efficacy of β₂-agonists in acute asthma is well-established, making this a historical comparison. Two studies reported a benefit of β₂-agonists over MgSO₄ alone for PEFR, while two studies found no difference. These results were not pooled. Hospital admissions were reported by only one small study, and events were rare, leading to an uncertain result. No serious adverse events were reported in any of the studies, although one small study reported mild to moderate adverse events with imprecise results. Authors' Conclusions: Nebulized MgSO₄ may provide modest additional benefits for lung function and hospital admission when added to inhaled β₂-agonists and ipratropium bromide. However, the confidence in this evidence is low, and substantial uncertainty remains. Recent large, well-designed trials have generally not demonstrated clinically significant benefits. Nebulized MgSO₄ does not appear to increase the risk of serious adverse events. Some individual studies suggest that patients with more severe asthma attacks or shorter attack durations may derive greater benefit, but further research into these subgroups is needed. Despite including 25 trials in this review, data pooling for all outcomes of interest was not possible, limiting the strength of the conclusions. A standardized core outcome set for studies in acute asthma is necessary, particularly for pediatric studies where lung function measurements during exacerbations may be challenging. Placebo-controlled trials in patients who do not respond to maximal standard treatment—including inhaled β₂-agonists, ipratropium bromide, and systemic steroids—may help clarify the role of nebulized MgSO₄ in acute asthma. However, the accumulating evidence suggests that a substantial benefit is unlikely.
